items.question: Why do you see the S4 correspondence as key to understanding how training data shapes a neural network’s behavior?
items.object: The S4 correspondence between training data, loss geometry, learning dynamics, and model weights
items.answer: I think the key question is: where does neural network behavior ultimately come from? All of our alignment techniques, what we're trying to do is change model behavior and make sure that they generalize robustly out of distribution. Many problems can be reduced to this understanding. Ultimately, behavior comes from training data, right? There are basically three inputs to every learning process: the neural network architecture, some choice of optimizer, and the training data. Of these, training data is the most important one, the one that tells one model to learn one algorithm and another model to learn a different algorithm. What we'd like to understand is how training data gives rise to the final behaviors models end up with, particularly because all of our current alignment techniques look like this. RLHF, Constitutional AI, DPO, deliberative alignment: all of these techniques are basically just modifications on the same deep learning processes with different data. In particular, data determines the geometry of the loss landscape. That geometry in turn tells SGD how to move around. It tells your optimization process how to move. That learning process picks out the final weights and thus the algorithms that a neural network ends up with. The structures in those weights determine how models generalize and thus whether they're aligned or not. This central dogma, as you called it, is something we called the S4 correspondence: between structure in data, structure in geometry, structure in the learning process, and structure in the final weights of the model. We see that as key to understanding the mapping from data to final behaviors.

items.question: How do you understand the role of degeneracy in a neural network’s loss landscape in determining how well it generalizes?
items.object: Degeneracy in neural network loss landscapes and its relationship to generalization
items.answer: I'd like to offer a slightly higher-level description. Usually, when people imagine what the loss landscape looks like at the bottom, or look at these slices, it'll look like a basin, a roundish basin like a parabola. What Dan calls degeneracy is the property that this is the wrong way to think about it. There are valleys and canyons and directions you can walk along that don't change the loss. In a sense, SLT tells us these are the most important directions by far. It's the number of valleys you have that determines how well your model generalizes. If there are more valleys, you can perturb your weights and change your implementation without actually changing the function you've implemented. That means your function is actually simpler. Simple functions can be implemented in more different ways. Through an Occam's razor kind of argument, it's the simplest function which generalizes best. We can make that statement very precise using SLT.

items.question: How do you think loss-landscape geometry can help distinguish algorithms that look identical on training data but generalize differently?
items.object: Loss-landscape geometry as a way to distinguish algorithms with different generalization behavior
items.answer: One thing we're worried about is your model might learn two algorithms that look identical from the training data, but one of them generalizes in a way that you don't like and one generalizes in a way that you do like. How do you distinguish them? What Dan's just saying is that maybe if you look at the neighborhood in the loss landscape, they actually have different geometries associated with them. This is the sense in which reading this geometry gives you information about what kind of algorithm you actually end up with.

items.question: How do you explain the selection between memorization and generalization in your essential dynamics study of transformers learning in-context linear regression?
items.object: Essential dynamics and the trade-off between memorization and generalization
items.answer:
What Dan was referring to as ED stands for essential dynamics. This is a paper we put out earlier this year where you can train a neural network, a transformer, to do in-context linear regression. You can give it X, Y, X, Y, X, Y samples and ask it to predict the Ys from the Xs, where each Y is generated from a simple linear transformation of the Xs plus some noise. What happens is, if you train it on lots and lots of different samples, the model will learn to do regression over the course of context. However, you can vary the number of distinct tasks that the model is exposed to during training. If you expose it to many different tasks, it learns regression. If you expose it to only a few different tasks, it'll memorize those tasks and won't learn the regression solution; it'll learn this memorization solution. Which solution the model ends up with varies as you vary the complexity or diversity of the number of tasks, and you see a phase transition where the model initially memorizes and then eventually learns this other solution.

You can try to understand the selection process between these using singular learning theory. Each solution has an associated performance and complexity. Memorization is always better at performance than this regression solution, which I call the generalization or meta-learning solution. The generalization solution, however, is simpler past a certain level of things that you have to memorize. So the simplest solution roughly occupies more volume in parameter space and is therefore easier to find. You notice this phenomenon where the model will first learn the generalizing solution, the simple one, before moving to the memorization solution. You can classify exactly which kinds of dynamics qualitatively you should expect to see based on this trade-off between performance and complexity, where complexity is reflected in the degeneracy of the loss landscape. It's kind of the opposite of grokking.

items.question: How do you view grokking as an example of how memorization and generalization interact?
items.answer: Well, grokking is actually a strange phenomenon. It's not typical. I think there's been, in a sense, overfitting to the example of grokking. In our opinion, this is not the typical way in which memorization and generalization interact.

The response suggests that understanding of memorization and generalization has relied too heavily on the example of grokking.

items.question: Why do you find alchemy a useful analogy for current deep learning?
items.answer: I think it's useful to compare current deep learning to alchemy. We've got some huge cauldron that's the architecture. We've got a fire that's the optimizer. Then we've got the reagents we put in this cauldron that we start to mix together; those reagents are the training data. Currently we just throw the entire internet together into this cauldron, start stirring, and hope that we haven't accidentally mixed bleach and Clorox.

Currently we just throw the entire internet together into this cauldron, start stirring, and hope that we haven't accidentally mixed bleach and Clorox.

rubrics.text: The response characterizes current deep-learning training as combining data without knowing whether the mixture will produce harmful interactions.

items.question: How do you envision AI training becoming more like industrial chemical manufacturing?
items.object: The future of AI training as industrial chemical manufacturing
items.answer: What we have in mind for the future of training looks more like industrial chemical manufacturing, where you know exactly which reagents you're mixing together, at what concentration, at what point in the process, and with what catalysts and ingredients. This level of control isn't accessible to us right now, but it's something we're already empirically starting to develop. We've split the post-training process into a bunch of different stages. There's chain-of-thought RL1, a second stage of chain-of-thought RL, a little bit of instruction fine-tuning, maybe Constitutional AI1 somewhere, a second stage of Constitutional AI just for the personality, then maybe more refusal training. Similarly, on the pretraining side, the process is being split into multiple stages so that we're developing an empirical understanding of how to better control the learning process. We think it's possible to develop the kind of scientific understanding to know when you should mix two samples in a batch together to get the desired behavior out the other end. This will give you more control over the entire process and what you end up with.

items.question: How do you see TUS's role in advancing singular learning theory for AI alignment?
items.answer:
TUS does two main things. Primarily, we're a research organization. In particular, the SLT for alignment agenda is sort of split into two parts. There's the more fundamental, theoretically heavy side, and that's work that Daniel Mur and his students are really focusing on. TUS is gearing more towards applications: taking these tools, scaling them up to frontier models as quickly as possible, trying to make progress that's meaningful to safety as quickly as possible. That's the work we're doing: experiments, training lots of models, running learning coefficient sweeps. That's one of these techniques we have from SLT that we use all over the place. Research is also maybe the primary thing that I'm doing. In addition to the research, we're also making sure to do outreach, to make sure that people are familiar with the work we're doing, so that at some future date we can hand off techniques to the labs, to policymakers, to other people who need to make decisions with what the current state of learning theory can do.

That outreach looks like me giving a lot of talks. Some of it looks like personalized outreach: thinking about other people's research agendas, questions they might have that SLT could contribute to, thinking about how to answer that, and then going up to those people and talking with them about it.

items.question: How do you distinguish developmental interpretability from the broader SLT for alignment agenda?
items.object: Developmental interpretability within the SLT for alignment agenda
items.answer:
Here are two different kinds of questions you can ask about that geometry. One is: over the course of training, how does the local geometry around my model change as I proceed? Are there qualitative changes in this local geometry that correlate with changes in the algorithm I'm implementing? Some work we've done so far shows that this seems to work. That's what I would call developmental interpretability: applying this lens of SLT to understanding the development process of neural networks, in particular because SLT makes some pretty concrete predictions about the kinds of allowed changes you'll see over the course of development, at least in a Bayesian setting. A lot of the work is in applying and seeing how much these predictions from the Bayesian setting transfer over to the SGD setting.

SLT developmental interpretability takes these tools from SLT and runs them over the course of development. But another question you can ask is just, what is this local geometry like for a given snapshot? Maybe a question like, how does this geometry, which depends on the data you're evaluating your model on, change as you change that distribution? If I change the distribution I'm evaluating my model and deploying my model on, do I see a qualitative change in the structure around my choice of weights? We expect that correlates with something like a change in the mode of computation on that data. It's a signal you can start to use to probe out-of-distribution generalization. Can you understand qualitatively the ways in which different structures in the model actually generalize? That doesn't necessarily require taking this developmental approach. In many cases they are synonymous, but there are questions you can ask that don't really fit the developmental frame.

items.question: What leads you to view the local learning coefficient as a potential measure of how much a model memorizes?
items.object: The local learning coefficient as a measure of memorization
items.answer:
One thing we've noticed is that SLT has this measure of model complexity called local learning coefficient, which you can see is an effective dimensionality, although in reality it's a richer metric than just effective dimensionality. This is something you can measure, and it depends on the data that you evaluate on. What we've noticed is it seems to correlate with something like memorization. In very recent work, we looked at a learning coefficient that tells you how much complexity there is in an attention head. What you find is that the learning coefficient correlates with the number of different n-grams or multigrams that a head has learned. The learning coefficient is higher if you've memorized more things.

There are other things like this. Work by Nina Paneri and Dimitri Viner looked at a grokking setting, and they looked at the size of the task that you're trying to memorize and how they change learning coefficient. There's a correlation there that's very, very clean. There's work on sparse parity tasks where you're looking at the number of different sparse parity tasks that your model is trying to memorize, and there's a correlation there. So there's starting to be, across a wide range of different things, some idea that we can measure how much a model is memorizing on the dataset.

items.question: How do you use the refined local learning coefficient to understand what attention heads specialize in?
items.object: Attention-head specialization revealed by the refined local learning coefficient
items.answer:
We have this measure of model complexity that tells you how much structure there is in the model as a whole, and how does that depend on the data? Two immediate refinements you can come up with on top of this learning coefficient from the theory: one of them is you change the dataset, so you don't evaluate on a pretraining dataset but some other dataset. The other thing you can do to refine it is to freeze some weights and measure the learning coefficient of a subset of weights. That's what I described with these attention heads. You can measure complexity, the amount of structure in a component of the model.

What you now notice is that if you incorporate this data refinement, you can start to say something about what different heads are specialized to, not just that different heads are different, but the ways in which they're different, what kinds of datasets they might be more important on. Induction, when you evaluate it on a code-heavy dataset, jumps up, so now the induction heads relatively experienced an increase in complexity. Moreover, they split apart. The induction heads previously look like they're sort of doing the same thing; evaluated on code, now there's a separation where one of them seems to be more important for code. Under additional analysis, you find that indeed this thing seems to be specialized to syntax tokens, punctuation, that kind of thing. So you've got tools that are starting to probe when two different structures are actually different, what it is specialized to. This feeds into the discovery of a new kind of circuit, which we call the multigram circuit.

items.question: How did you interpret the apparent migration of multigram information between layers when investigating the multigram circuit?
items.answer:
We still don't fully understand this model. There's still work to be done, but what seems to happen first is heads individually memorize n-grams and skips become multigram heads, and this seems to go faster in the first layer. In the second layer, what you notice is that the learning coefficient, a particular kind of refined learning coefficient where you're measuring how similar performance is to some baseline one-layer model, which you treat as a reference for what n-gram behavior is like, peaks after the second stage of development. At that point, this starts to decrease for the first layer, but it's still increasing for the second layer. So theoretically the model seems to be losing information about multigram prediction in the first layer.

You can verify this in a handful of cases where you actually notice a migration, for example, of a multigram from layer one to layer two. But you also notice that now the tokens that different heads seem to be involved in are changing, and now there's coordination. One of the layer one heads seems to be very involved in the same kinds of tokens, and a different layer two head is doing it. You can actually verify by certain kinds of ablations and path ablations, where you only ablate the outputs of these heads into the input of this head in the second layer, that it needs coordination. The model is actually passing information forward now to second-layer heads in order to predict nested pattern matching. That wasn't the case before.

We're still using ablations to verify that there's coordination going on here. We're looking at certain kinds of composition scores to verify that layer one is feeding into layer two; they're reading and writing from the same subspace. There's other analyses where we're looking, if you ablate this head, which tokens are maximally affected across the dataset, and actually looking at a bunch of those examples. All of that analysis is going into identifying a multigram circuit. This observation that information might be migrating from layer one to layer two is something that can set you off, and I think that's something that we'll observe more generally as we scale up to larger models, these kinds of signals.
